gaps.quote: Undoing the exchange moves each output back to its input role, and multiplying by $\varepsilon_w$ again removes the sign.
gaps.note: The page never says the network consists of the exchange followed by an undoing pass, what the undoing network is, or what operator the combined forward-and-undo route applies. The frames of the undoing routes are not given, so the reader cannot check that anything is restored; the page also never states the final result the network computes on the array.

gaps.quote: For a scratch role the construction has $\rho(w)=w$ with sign $+1$ (cited), so the undoing needs no correction there.
gaps.note: 'The construction' of the network is never described, so the cited fact that scratch roles have rho(w)=w and sign +1 stands in for how the concept works. Even so, such a route applies D_sink(w) D_source(w)^{-1}, which is not the identity unless the two frames agree, so 'needs no correction' is not justified.

gaps.term: every role keeps endpoint operator vs restoration
gaps.quote: Every role keeps the endpoint operator (cited), auxiliary roles included.
gaps.note: This conflicts with the opening claim that the network 'restores every auxiliary value it uses': if an auxiliary role keeps a nontrivial endpoint operator D_sink D_source^{-1}, its value is not restored. The statement needs the hypothesis that source and sink frames of auxiliary roles coincide, or the opening should say values are restored only up to the endpoint operator. The cited claim's content and role are not explained.

gaps.quote: its operator is $D_\nu$, however many gates it passes through
gaps.note: The page just derived that a route applies epsilon_w D_sink D_source^{-1}. With source frame I and sink frame D_nu the operator is epsilon_w D_nu, not D_nu; the example is correct only for sign +1 (for instance a scratch role).
